vignette:
She is a 37-year-old South Eastern Asian woman who works as a refugee aid worker, and the story she tells about how she came to need help begins with a night that still feels unfinished to her. She is married now, and her husband is one of the few people with whom she can speak openly, but even with him she often stops short of the worst parts. Before the incident, she describes herself as practical, steady, and able to sit with other people’s pain without being overwhelmed by it. Her work took her into crowded settlement offices, temporary shelters, and border areas where families arrived with little more than bags and documents. She had long believed that if she stayed calm, used the right words, and knew the rules, she could help keep people safe.

The event that changes this is police violence during an operation near a refugee gathering point. She is there as part of her work, trying to assist a family who has been told they may be relocated. The scene moves quickly and then, in her memory, freezes in fragments: shouting, boots on the ground, a baton lifted, someone crying out, a child clinging to a mother’s skirt. She remembers the particular smell of dust and sweat, the sharp metallic sense of fear in her mouth, and the shock of realizing that the uniforms she had associated with order were instead the source of danger. She does not describe herself as heroic in that moment; she says she was mostly trying not to be seen, not to make things worse, not to be the next person struck. Still, she cannot forget the look on the faces of the families around her, a kind of confused disbelief that turns into panic. What lingers most is not only what happened to others, but the helplessness of being an educated adult with experience in the field and finding that none of it mattered when violence arrived.

Afterward, she goes back to work because that is what she knows how to do. On the outside she appears composed, even efficient, but colleagues notice that she becomes quieter and more easily startled. She begins checking exits automatically when she enters a room. If a door slams or a car backfires, her body jolts before her mind can catch up. She keeps her voice low in meetings, as if loudness itself might summon trouble. On the way to field sites, she scans for police vehicles and feels her chest tighten when she sees uniforms clustered near checkpoints. She tells herself she is simply being cautious, but the caution has the feel of vigilance that never rests.

At night the memory returns in pieces. Sometimes she wakes with her heart pounding, convinced she hears shouting outside. Other times she falls asleep and dreams of running through a narrow corridor with no exit, or of being unable to find the child from that day. In the morning she feels exhausted, as if she has spent the whole night bracing for impact. She avoids news footage of protests or arrests because even a brief image can leave her unsettled for hours. She also notices herself pulling away from conversations about the work she once loved. When other aid workers speak passionately about advocacy, she feels both guilty and numb. There is a part of her that still cares deeply, but it is harder now to access that part without also feeling fear.

Her marriage has become both a refuge and a place where she worries about burdening someone else. Her husband sees that she is not the same, though he does not push her. She appreciates his patience and then feels ashamed for needing it. She has moments of irritability that surprise her; small frustrations at home can feel disproportionately sharp, followed by remorse. She is often on edge in crowds, especially when she cannot identify who is in charge or whether she can leave quickly. She still performs her job well enough that others assume she is coping, but internally she feels split between the person who continues to show up for refugees and the person who flinches at every sudden movement.

Over several sessions, she describes a growing sadness beneath the fear. The violence has not only frightened her; it has damaged the assumptions that once gave her work meaning. She no longer feels certain that safety can be negotiated, that authority can be trusted, or that competence is always enough to protect the vulnerable. Even so, she keeps returning to the places and people who need her, carrying her fear alongside her professional resolve, trying to make sense of a world that became much less predictable on that day and has never fully returned to what it was before.
